summary.text: A state of matter is one of the distinct forms matter can take, and four are seen in everyday life: solid, liquid, gas and plasma.
States differ in how their particles are arranged and behave together: packed in fixed spots in a solid, close but sliding in a liquid, far apart and free in a gas.
Beyond these four are many other states, such as liquid crystals, magnetic states, and Bose–Einstein condensates in extreme cold.

facts.value: Fifteen known crystal structures at various temperatures and pressures

facts.value: Gas-like, plus charged particles that respond to electric and magnetic fields

items.prompt: You pour juice from a tall glass into a wide bowl. It takes the bowl's shape, yet the amount stays the same. What is going on among its particles?

options.label: They sit locked in fixed positions inside the bowl
They stay close together but slide past one another
They spread far apart to fill all the bowl's space
They become charged and respond to magnetic fields

items.explain: In a liquid the particles stay close but can move past one another, so the volume stays fixed while the shape follows the container.

items.prompt: A small puff of gas is released in one corner of a sealed room. What does it end up doing?

options.label: Spreading out until it fills the whole room
Staying in its corner with a clear edge
Settling into a thin layer on the floor
Keeping its own shape while drifting around

items.explain: A gas expands to fill the shape and volume of its container, so it occupies the entire room.

items.prompt: Water ice can form many different crystal structures at different pressures and temperatures. How do scientists classify these?

options.label: As different states, one for each crystal structure
As liquids that have only partly frozen
As different phases that all belong to the solid state
As forms of plasma created under pressure

items.explain: Ice is the solid state of water, yet it has multiple phases with different crystal structures, so one state can contain many phases.

items.prompt: A substance turns straight from a solid into a gas, never becoming a liquid on the way. Is that possible?

options.label: No, a solid must melt before it can boil
No, only liquids are able to become gases
Yes, but only after it first becomes a plasma
Yes, the process is called sublimation

items.explain: Solids can change directly into gases through sublimation, and gases can change directly into solids through deposition.

items.prompt: A coffee maker wants a dense, gas-like fluid that can dissolve caffeine out of beans. Which kind of substance fits?

options.label: A plasma produced by a huge voltage difference
A vapor liquefied by compression alone
A supercritical fluid above critical temperature and pressure
An ordinary gas held at low pressure

items.explain: A supercritical fluid has the properties of a gas but is dense enough to act as a solvent; supercritical carbon dioxide is used to extract caffeine.

items.prompt: A scientist wants to turn an ordinary gas into the electrically charged state. What could she do?

options.label: Cool it until its particles barely move
Run a huge voltage across it or heat it extremely hot
Compress it until it turns into a liquid
Let it expand into a much larger container

items.explain: A gas is usually converted to a plasma by a huge voltage difference between two points or by extremely high temperatures.

pack.title: Same stuff, different behavior
pack.question: Why do solids, liquids and gases act so differently?

beats.title: Same stuff, different behavior
beats.hook: Some matter keeps its shape, some flows to fit a container, and some fills every corner.

beats.prompt: You pour a liquid from a tall glass into a wide bowl. What happens to its shape and its amount?
beats.explain: Liquid particles stay close together but slide past one another, so the volume is fixed while the shape follows the container.

choices.label: It spreads to fill the whole bowl, and the amount grows
choices.feedback: That is what a gas does; a liquid keeps a fixed volume.

choices.label: It takes the bowl's shape, and the amount stays the same
It keeps the glass's tall shape, and the amount stays the same
choices.feedback: Tempting because a solid behaves this way, but liquid particles can move past one another and adapt to the container.

beats.prompt: Match each state to how its particles behave.

right.label: Contains charged ions and free electrons
Close together but able to move past one another

beats.explain: The states are told apart by how their particles are arranged and how they behave collectively.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?

steps.text: Ice is the solid state of water.
Ice has fifteen known crystal structures, formed at different pressures and temperatures.
So each of those structures must be its own state of matter.
Therefore water has at least fifteen states.

beats.explain: Different crystal structures are different phases within the same state, here the solid state.

beats.prompt: A beaker of liquid sits at a steady temperature. Without heating it, how could you turn it into a gas?
beats.explain: A liquid may become a gas by reducing the pressure at constant temperature.

choices.label: Cool it until it solidifies
choices.feedback: Cooling moves a liquid toward a solid, not a gas.

choices.label: Raise the pressure around it
choices.feedback: Compression works the other way: below the critical temperature it can liquefy a vapor.

beats.idea: The difference is how tightly the particles are packed and how freely they move.

paragraphs.heading: What a state of matter is
paragraphs.text: A state of matter, also called a phase of matter, is one of the separate forms that matter can take. Four of them turn up in ordinary life: solid, liquid, gas and plasma. What sets them apart is how their tiny parts, such as atoms, molecules, ions and electrons, are laid out and how they behave as a group.

paragraphs.heading: Solids
paragraphs.text: In a solid, the particles are packed tightly and stay in fixed spots. The pull between them is so strong that they cannot wander off, only vibrate where they are. That is why a solid keeps a set shape and a set volume, and changes shape only when an outside force breaks or cuts it. In crystalline solids the particles sit in a regular, repeating pattern, and one substance can have more than one such pattern. Iron, for example, switches from one cubic arrangement to another at 912 °C.

paragraphs.heading: Liquids
paragraphs.text: In a liquid, the particles stay close but can slide past each other. The forces between them still matter, yet the particles have enough energy to move around, so the structure is mobile. A liquid therefore takes the shape of whatever holds it while keeping a nearly constant volume, and it is very hard to squeeze. A liquid usually takes up more room than the same substance as a solid, and water, H₂O, is the best known exception.

paragraphs.heading: Gases and plasma
paragraphs.text: Gas particles sit far from one another and roam freely. They carry so much energy of motion that the forces between them have little effect, and the gap between neighbours is much larger than the particles themselves. A gas is a fluid that can be squeezed into less space. It has no set shape or volume, and spreads out to fill its whole container. Plasma is like a gas, but it also holds charged particles, ions and free electrons, that move on their own and respond to electric and magnetic fields.

paragraphs.heading: Changing state
paragraphs.text: Matter can move from one state to another. Melting turns a solid into a liquid, and freezing does the reverse. A solid can also skip the liquid stage and become a gas directly, which is called sublimation, while the jump back from gas to solid is called deposition. Heating a liquid to its boiling point, or lowering the pressure on it, turns it into a gas. A gas usually becomes a plasma either through a huge voltage between two points or through extremely high temperatures.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond the classic four
paragraphs.text: Many more states exist beyond these four. Some sit in between: liquid crystals behave partly like solids and partly like liquids. Magnetic states depend not on where the atoms are but on how their built-in magnetic moments, called spins, line up. Others appear only in extreme conditions, such as Bose–Einstein condensates in extreme cold, or quark–gluon plasma at extremely high energy.

paragraphs.heading: Phases within a state
paragraphs.text: The word phase is sometimes used to mean a state of matter, but one substance can form several phases while staying in the same state. Ice is solid water, yet it has fifteen known crystal structures that form at different temperatures and pressures. The line between liquid and gas can blur too. Above its critical temperature and critical pressure, a gas becomes a supercritical fluid, in which liquid and gas can no longer be told apart. Supercritical carbon dioxide is used to remove caffeine when making decaffeinated coffee.
